title: Archer Maclean's Mercury
subtitle: Tilt the world beneath a drop of liquid metal
summary: Archer Maclean's Mercury is Awesome Studios' PSP puzzle-platform game, first released in North America on 6 April 2005. body: Archer Maclean's Mercury is Awesome Studios' PSP puzzle-platform game, first released in North America on 6 April 2005. The player tilts a stage to guide a drop of mercury towards its destination. Unlike a solid ball, the material can stretch and divide, making its physical behaviour part of the problem. A narrow passage or exposed edge has to be approached with an awareness of what the liquid will do next. The game asks for careful control of the surroundings rather than direct movement of a character, giving gravity the role of the player's intermediary.

Tilting changes the direction and momentum of the mercury, so reaching a safe position often means beginning to slow it before the destination is reached. Different stages emphasise different tasks and obstacles, asking the player to adapt the same physical control to another arrangement. The unusual material gives an ordinary slope more consequences than it would have for a rigid object. The player has to watch the shape of the drop as well as its location, treating the stage as something that can pull the liquid apart or carry it towards the goal.

Archer Maclean developed the idea from a small activity in Jimmy White's Cueball World, adding liquid-metal behaviour to create a distinct puzzle. An intended tilt-sensor accessory for PSP did not reach release because of technical limitations, leaving the finished game controlled through the handheld's ordinary inputs. Reviews welcomed the concept and level design while noting the difficulty. Its success led to Mercury Meltdown and Mercury Hg. The original's clarity comes from a recognisable physical action: alter the slope, observe the material and make the next adjustment before momentum turns a useful movement into a loss.

A physics experiment becomes a portable puzzle series
